articles.text: Piedmont teachers gathered outside their school sites during student drop-off on Tuesday morning, August 23, to bring awareness to their upcoming salary negotiations with the school district, scheduled for Monday, August 29. Teachers are pleading for salary increases to help them cope with 9% inflation and the difficulty of being able to afford living in the Bay Area. At all Piedmont school sites teachers demonstrated their support by wearing red and waving signs asking for community support. A similar rally was held at schools last spring. Salary negotiations between the Association of Piedmont Teachers, the teachers’ union, and the district office broke off in May 2022 with no agreement. Teachers returned to their classrooms this fall without any salary increase. The last two years have seen record numbers of teachers resigning in Piedmont, including one who resigned just days before the start of this school year because other districts offered $30,000 more than Piedmont’s salary. Over the summer Piedmont School District’s budget showed a surplus of $2,200,000 as the state of California projected a record $128 billion going to schools. Historically, Piedmont teachers receive small raises typically 1-3%, but this year their message is loud and clear: larger action is needed. A teacher shortage throughout the state has existed for nearly three years, since the start of the pandemic. Many Piedmont teachers see the issue as simple economics: the increase in demand should increase their value. Middle school teachers prior to the start of the school day rallied in front of the school to highlight the need for teacher raises.
articles.title: Teachers rally for raises ahead of Monday’s salary negotiations

articles.text: PRFO campaign aims to close construction funding gap The city of Piedmont will launch a campaign focused on funding 20 heat pumps required to heat the new Piedmont Community Pool using electricity. The city council approved the authorization to proceed with fundraising efforts at an August 15 meeting. “Cost estimates have held steady since the significant design revisions undertaken in March to combat construction hyperinflation. Based on council direction in May… we will proceed with an all-electric facility,” said City Administrator Sara Lillevand. The overall estimated construction funding gap is $2.1 million. “When we add in all the safety maintenance and competitive equipment, as a well as a timing scoreboard and sports lighting, we are projecting a total potential funding gap of $2.6 million to deliver the community pool facility,” Lillevand said. “These are projections based on estimates, and we won’t know the real costs until we open [construction firm] bids in six to eight weeks.” Funding for the project will primarily come from Measure UU General Obligations Bonds; to front the added costs, the Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization (PRFO) is ready to launch a robust community pool fundraising campaign with donor levels and potential naming opportunities within the facility, Lillevand explained. “This has the potential to close the entire funding gap,” she said. articles.text: Drought is an urgent issue for Piedmont Editor: The city of Piedmont is making an effort to reduce the city’s carbon footprint, which is commendable. However, there is a more urgent and immediate issue we’re not addressing, and that is the drought. I believe the city should start a campaign urging people to reduce their water consumption and the wasteful use of water. Looking around, you see more lawns in Piedmont than anywhere in other East Bay cities. I know it’s not up to Piedmont to set limits – that’s up to EBMUD and the state – but as responsible citizens we must realize how critical it is to save water, and not just by putting bricks in our toilet tanks. At the very least, reduce the number of days you water those lawns, and lower the amount of water per day. If you see water running down the street, you’re watering too much. If you see your neighbors watering too much, consider saying something about it. Even better, remove lawns and replace them with native plants, which use far less water, and attract native insects and birds. We should acknowledge that we live in a partial desert. Consider creating dry gardens with succulents and cacti. I realize that, even if EBMUD raises rates for overuse, many of us in Piedmont can afford to pay whatever it costs to keep those lush green lawns. But we must think of others less fortunate and help reduce our wasteful use of water before severe quotas are mandated for everybody. A number of towns and counties in the North Bay are close to running out of water. The Colorado River and the two largest reservoirs it supplies are running at the lowest levels in history. Even Los Angeles with its thousands of swimming pools, may have to initiate water rationing. – Ken Greenberg Piedmont

articles.text: An algal bloom in Lake Merritt prompted Oakland Public Works Department to post warning signs along the lakeshore near the 1200 to 1400 blocks of Lakeshore Avenue on August 4. The agency warned the public that low levels of contaminants associated with the algal bloom have been discovered and cautioned pedestrians, children and pets to stay away from the water. On August 4, Oakland Public Works received a report from a concerned resident of brownish red water in the lake. “The reddish color of the material in the water indicates it could be a Cyanobacteria bloom, also known as a harmful algal bloom, which can produce toxins that are harmful to humans and animals,” the agency said in a press release. “Oakland Public Works staff are conducting additional inspection of the area and will submit a report to the San Francisco Bay Regional Water Quality Control Board.” Oakland city staff have confirmed that ongoing testing will continue. The most recent scheduled testing date was Monday, August 22. The algal bloom is potentially caused by increased inputs of nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilizers and human or animal wastes, low water flows, stagnant water, increased intensity and duration of sunlight, and sustained high temperatures, the City of Oakland explained in a press release, adding that current research suggests that the rising temperatures and changing precipitation patterns caused by climate change are a catalyst for their growth. The Alameda County Environmental Health Department issued a similar warning. “It is highly recommended that people and their pets stay out of the water until the blooms dissipate,” said the Alameda County Environmental Health Department in a statement. “Contact with the algae blooms can cause skin irritation and burning eyes to humans and can cause more dangerous effects to dogs.” The algal phenomenon is occurring throughout the Bay Area, said San Francisco Baykeeper Executive Director Sejal Choksi-Chugh. San Francisco Baykeeper is an environmental group based in Oakland that has investigated marine pollution in the Bay and its watershed since 1989. The group’s team of lawyers, scientists, and environmental activists have worked to strengthen laws that protect Bay Area waters and hold polluters accountable. Choksi-Chugh explained that, after conducting tests of impacted areas, that the algal bloom is caused by a bacteria known as Heterosigma akashiwo. “Our scientists have been monitoring the situation and are in communication with relevant agencies and researchers. Both the California Department of Public Health and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration have identified the dominant algal species forming the bloom as Heterosigma akashiwo– a species known to form ‘red tides’,” said Choksi-Chugh. “The US Geological Service and San Francisco Estuary Institute report high densities of H. akashiwo further south, as far as Newark.” The algal bloom in Lake Merritt and the Oakland Estuary extends across the East Bay’s shoreline, including to the Richmond and Berkeley marinas and the Albany Bulb, San Francisco, and into the South Bay. Although the City of Oakland has not yet released the findings of its August 22 test, the city and San Francisco Baykeeper warns against coming in contact with the water.
articles.title: Algal bloom in Lake Merritt; public asked to stay away

articles.text: Virtually all statewide and citywide mandates on masking and showing proof of vaccination have been lifted as of April 2022, two years after Gov. Gavin Newsom issued a state of emergency in response to the COVID pandemic. These safety protocols are still required in limited settings. According to the California Department of Public Health (CDPH), masks are required in public healthcare settings, emergency shelters, jails and prisons, homeless shelters, and long-term care facilities. Schools The state has lifted its mask mandate in schools. However, both the CDPH and Piedmont Unified School District have issued statements advising that masks are strongly recommended. “While there are no current indoor masking requirements for schools in California or Alameda County, the wearing of masks in indoor school settings remains strongly recommended. All students and staff are encouraged to wear masks indoors, and in any situation where social distancing is limited,” said Piedmont Interim School Superintendent Dr. Donald Evans. Proof of vaccination against COVID is no longer required in Piedmont public schools. The CDPH announced in April that it would no longer include the COVID-19 vaccine in its list of mandated childhood vaccines for public schools. Piedmont School District mandated COVID-19 vaccination for all students from kindergarten through 12th grade in September 2021. On April 27, Alameda County Superior Court Judge Brad Seligman struck down the case, which led to a settlement agreement. Under the agreement, the school district cannot consider any similar mandates in the future. “COVID vaccinations remain the best defense against the virus and a valuable tool in keeping our schools open,” said Dr. Evans. “We thank our community for its partnership in helping create a safer school environment by receiving COVID vaccinations and boosters at one of the highest percentages in the country. PUSD continues to strongly recommend all who are eligible to get vaccinated.” Traveling Masks are not required, but are strongly recommended for California public transit riders, and commuters in stations, terminals, and airports. The Centers for Disease Control no longer enforces masking on public transportation conveyances and at transit hubs at the federal level. U.S District Judge Kathryn Kimball Mizelle in Tampa struck down the requirement in April, ruling that the CDC had overstepped its authority in issuing a mask mandate on transportation. The CDC responded in a brief asking the appeals court to reverse the district’s court decision. “It is difficult to imagine a more direct way to control the spread of communicable disease than a measure that traps infectious particles to prevent their spread,” the agency stated. The U.S. Justice Department filed the brief as part of the case appeal to the U.S 11th Circuit Court Appeals and added that the law granting CDC authority to rollout public safety mandates has been “used to prohibit the capture, distribution, or release of certain animals to prevent the spread of monkeypox.” “I’m at the point where I can’t remember the difference between net and gross.”
articles.title: Where masks & vaccines are still required in California

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is offering free compost for Piedmont residents. The site is open every Friday and will be open, weather and conditions permitting, each Friday after 8:00 a.m. The compost is first-come, first-served, and City staff cannot guarantee or confirm availability of compost. The compost originally comes from the green waste (yard trimmings and food waste) that is collected in Republic Services communities participating in curbside organics collection services, which includes the City of Piedmont. The green waste is brought to a processing plant in Richmond where it is converted into a highly aerobic, microbial compost. The compost making process involves the careful mixing of the waste and monitoring of the carbon to nitrogen ratio, Carbon dioxide, temperature, and moisture. As the compost is locally based and free, it models the concept of a circular economy, where a resource is used and reused in a cycle that turns “waste” back into new products Staff photo The compost is available in a dumpster box located near the entrance to the City’s Corporation Yard located at 898 Red Rock Road. or materials than can reenter the supply chain. This process helps to keep organic materials from emitting greenhouse gasses in the landfill and creates opportunities to use these nutrient-rich resources to regenerate our soils. Mixing compost with your soil also aids in water retention and pest control and helps plants thrive. To pick up compost, bring a shovel, a container, and gloves for loading the material. Pickup trucks must use a tarp covering. The compost is available in a dumpster box located near the entrance to the City’s Corporation Yard located at 898 Red Rock Road. pages.text: Wednesday, August 24, 2022 3 Algal bloom in Lake Merritt; public asked to stay away By Allyson Aleksey An algal bloom in Lake Merritt prompted Oakland Public Works Department to post warning signs along the lakeshore near the 1200 to 1400 blocks of Lakeshore Avenue on August 4. The agency warned the public that low levels of contaminants associated with the algal bloom have been discovered and cautioned pedestrians, children and pets to stay away from the water. On August 4, Oakland Public Works received a report from a concerned resident of brownish red water in the lake. “The reddish color of the material in the water indicates it could be a Cyanobacteria bloom, also known as a harmful algal bloom, which can produce toxins that are harmful to humans and animals,” the agency said in a press release. “Oakland Public Works staff are conducting additional inspection of the area and will submit a report to the San Francisco Bay Regional Water Quality Control Board.” Oakland city staff have confirmed that ongoing testing will continue. The most recent scheduled testing date was Monday, August 22. The algal bloom is potentially caused by increased inputs of nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilizers and human or animal wastes, low water flows, stagnant water, increased intensity and duration of sunlight, and sustained high temperatures, the City of Oakland explained in a press release, adding that current research suggests that the rising temperatures and changing precipitation patterns caused by climate change are a catalyst for their growth. The Alameda County Environmental Health Department issued a similar warning. “It is highly recommended that people and their pets stay out of the water until the blooms dissipate,” said the Alameda County Environmental Health Department in a statement. “Contact with the algae blooms can cause skin irritation and burning eyes to humans and can cause more dangerous effects to dogs.” The algal phenomenon is occurring throughout the Bay Area, said San Francisco Baykeeper Executive Director Sejal Choksi-Chugh. San Francisco Baykeeper is an environmental group based in Oakland that has investigated marine pollution in the Bay and its watershed since 1989. The group’s team of lawyers, scientists, and environmental activists have worked to strengthen laws that protect Bay Area waters and hold polluters accountable. Choksi-Chugh explained that, after conducting tests of impacted areas, that the algal bloom is caused by a bacteria known as Heterosigma akashiwo. “Our scientists have been monitoring the situation and are in communication with relevant agencies and researchers. Both the California Department of Public Health and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration have identified the dominant algal species forming the bloom as Heterosigma akashiwo– a species known to form ‘red tides’,” said Choksi-Chugh. “The US Geological Service and San Francisco Estuary Institute report high densities of H. akashiwo further south, as far as Newark.” The algal bloom in Lake Merritt and the Oakland Estuary extends across the East Bay’s shoreline, including to the Richmond and Berkeley marinas and the Albany Bulb, San Francisco, and into the South Bay. Although the City of Oakland has not yet released the findings of its August 22 test, the city and San Francisco Baykeeper warns against coming in contact with the water. Free compost at city Corp. Yard this Friday The City of Piedmont is offering free compost for Piedmont residents. The site is open every Friday and will be open, weather and conditions permitting, each Friday after 8:00 a.m. The compost is first-come, first-served, and City staff cannot guarantee or confirm availability of compost. The compost originally comes from the green waste (yard trimmings and food waste) that is collected in Republic Services communities participating in curbside organics collection services, which includes the City of Piedmont. The green waste is brought to a processing plant in Richmond where it is converted into a highly aerobic, microbial compost. The compost making process involves the careful mixing of the waste and monitoring of the carbon to nitrogen ratio, Carbon dioxide, temperature, and moisture. As the compost is locally based and free, it models the concept of a circular economy, where a resource is used and reused in a cycle that turns “waste” back into new products Staff photo The compost is available in a dumpster box located near the entrance to the City’s Corporation Yard located at 898 Red Rock Road. or materials than can reenter the supply chain. This process helps to keep organic materials from emitting greenhouse gasses in the landfill and creates opportunities to use these nutrient-rich resources to regenerate our soils. Mixing compost with your soil also aids in water retention and pest control and helps plants thrive. To pick up compost, bring a shovel, a container, and gloves for loading the material. Pickup trucks must use a tarp covering. The compost is available in a dumpster box located near the entrance to the City’s Corporation Yard located at 898 Red Rock Road. Gavin Newsom issued a state of emergency in response to the COVID pandemic. These safety protocols are still required in limited settings. According to the California Department of Public Health (CDPH), masks are required in public healthcare settings, emergency shelters, jails and prisons, homeless shelters, and long-term care facilities. Schools The state has lifted its mask mandate in schools. However, both the CDPH and Piedmont Unified School District have issued statements advising that masks are strongly recommended. “While there are no current indoor masking requirements for schools in California or Alameda County, the wearing of masks in indoor school settings remains strongly recommended. All students and staff are encouraged to wear masks indoors, and in any situation where social distancing is limited,” said Piedmont Interim School Superintendent Dr. Donald Evans. Proof of vaccination against COVID is no longer required in Piedmont public schools. The CDPH announced in April that it would no longer include the COVID-19 vaccine in its list of mandated childhood vaccines for public schools. Piedmont School District mandated COVID-19 vaccination for all students from kindergarten through 12th grade in September 2021. On April 27, Alameda County Superior Court Judge Brad Seligman struck down the case, which led to a settlement agreement. Under the agreement, the school district cannot consider any similar mandates in the future. “COVID vaccinations remain the best defense against the virus and a valuable tool in keeping our schools open,” said Dr. Evans. “We thank our community for its partnership in helping create a safer school environment by receiving COVID vaccinations and boosters at one of the highest percentages in the country. PUSD continues to strongly recommend all who are eligible to get vaccinated.” Traveling Masks are not required, but are strongly recommended for California public transit riders, and commuters in stations, terminals, and airports. The Centers for Disease Control no longer enforces masking on public transportation conveyances and at transit hubs at the federal level. U.S District Judge Kathryn Kimball Mizelle in Tampa struck down the requirement in April, ruling that the CDC had overstepped its authority in issuing a mask mandate on transportation. The CDC responded in a brief asking the appeals court to reverse the district’s court decision. “It is difficult to imagine a more direct way to control the spread of communicable disease than a measure that traps infectious particles to prevent their spread,” the agency stated. The U.S. Justice Department filed the brief as part of the case appeal to the U.S 11th Circuit Court Appeals and added that the law granting CDC authority to rollout public safety mandates has been “used to prohibit the capture, distribution, or release of certain animals to prevent the spread of monkeypox.” READ IT IN THE POST “I’m at the point where I can’t remember the difference between net and gross.”

articles.text: Urban Compassion Project volunteers will gather this Saturday, August 27, at 5th and Webster Street in Oakland to assist with a weekly scheduled urban cleanup. The Project, founded by Vincent Ray Williams, hosts cleanups every Saturday morning at various locations in Oakland. Piedmont residents have joined Williams in his humble mission since the group’s inception. The organization seeks to build community between the unhoused and housed community through these simple acts of kindness. The volunteer-led grassroots effort started under the name Urban Park Cleanup and has since expanded to provide a variety of resources for the unhoused community of Oakland. “We approach [cleanups] with compassion and kindness and build bridges between volunteers and our unhoused community,” said Williams. The cleanup will be held from 9 a.m. to 12 p.m. Volunteers should wear a mask, closed-toe shoes and gloves. All cleaning supplies are provided by Urban Compassion Project, and donations are always welcome. articles.text: Piedmont’s Boy Scouts of America (BSA) council sent its Order of the Arrow (OA) Lodge to the University of Tennessee to participate in a week-long conference in August. Piedmont’s OA Lodge, Hungteetsepoppi, was one of over 250 lodges that participated in the National Order of the Arrow conference (NOAC). The Order of the Arrow was founded over 100 years ago to recognize Scouts who showed expertise in camping. It is now the recognized service arm in the BSA, dedicated to camping and service. Candidates are elected by their peers and wear a white sash with a red arrow to signify their membership in the OA. This 2022 conference had more than 6,500 members from across the country participating for a week of amazing activities and fellowship. articles.text: Piedmont continues to honor the 50th anniversary of the passage of Title IX, the federal law which guarantees that no person will be discriminated against on the basis of sex in their education, including school sports. Around town, you can see girls, women, and many boys and men showing their support for Title IX with their black and gold t-shirts and hoodies. Piedmont’s Title IX celebration committee is using the funds from the merchandise sales and donations to raise awareness about the law and to advocate for improvements for girls’ sports at PUSD. The Education Speaker Series kicks off this year on Tuesday, September 13, at 7:30 pm with Kim Turner, Positive Coaching Alliance’s Director of the Gender Equity Initiative, speaking about the Pursuit of Equity: Why Title IX Matters. She is a coach, athlete, advocate, and former nonprofit Title IX attorney who has spearheaded lawsuits around the country bringing school districts and universities into compliance with Title IX and affording hundreds of thousands of girls a chance at a full educational experience. “We’re excited to have Kim Turner this anniversary year of Title IX to educate the community and show our girls that they should have every opportunity in athletics just like the boys,” said Dana Lung, Piedmont Education Foundation board member and chair of the Education Speaker Series. “I’m proud to support Title IX,” said Dan Cavenaugh. “It is essential for our daughters to know and feel that their opportunities and experiences are the same as our sons. These impressions impact the trajectory of every aspect of their lives.” Even elementary students will learn about Title IX this year, as the celebration committee plans to use some of its funds to purchase age-appropriate books for each of PUSD’s school libraries. The books will be chosen by the school librarians and will include titles such as Nike is a Goddess: The History of Women in Sports. Meanwhile, the Title IX celebration committee continues to advocate for Piedmont School District to come into compliance with Title IX. The first-ever audit conducted by the school district over the course of 2021-22 showed significant deficiencies between the boys and girls athletic experiences in Piedmont. Piedmont offers 55 fewer slots for girls to participate in high school sports than boys. “Athletics provide significant benefits for girls and boys alike, and Piedmont girls want that opportunity,” said Mary Wells, a volunteer on the committee. “I´m happy the district conducted an audit last year and promised to follow up annually.” For those interested in buying a t-shirt or hoodie, sales at the Piedmont Store will continue through August 26. Tickets to the Title IX Education Speaker Series event may be purchased at https:// piedmontstore.org/ Stay tuned for details on the Appreciating Diversity Film Series, which will screen a pair of short documentaries (The Queen of Basketball and Mink!), and the spring of 2023 Readmont book, which will focus on Title IX.

articles.text: Highlands Preschool is in high gear preparing for a magical 2022-2023 school year. Director Deanna Johnson, well-known for her love of glitter and ability to make each and every child feel loved, is putting the final touches on this year’s curriculum. Along with Head Teacher Angela Livermore, Johnson ensures that Highland’s playbased curriculum is shaped in a way that celebrates the diverse array of holidays, customs, and cultures celebrated by the Highlands community. In addition, the teachers incorporate letters, words, numbers, and science into their lessons while staying true to the play-based philosophy of the school. Community is key to Highlands, a co-op preschool. Parents volunteer in the classroom and play an active role in their child’s experience. Having parents in the classroom helps make the classroom run more smoothly, keeps tuition low, strengthens the relationship between the home and school environments, and provides a window for parents to observe their child’s life at school. articles.text: Piedmont parents hosted a Back-to-School Carnival for all sixth graders at Piedmont Middle School on Thursday, August 18, the second week of school. A total of 175 students attended the optional afterschool event, replete with carnival games, sporting competitions, food and raffle prizes. articles.text: A large crowd gathered for last year’s Open House hosted by members of the Piedmont Community Service Crew. Teens and their parents are invited to attend an open house and Fall Kickoff hosted by the Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) on Sunday August 28 at 4 p.m. Sign up to attend at: https://forms.gle/4iJmyPA5CRrmmMcT7 Come meet current crew members and youth leaders. This will be a fun, social event with refreshments along with presentations about the crew and how members and their parents can benefit. Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC), a youth-led organization, provides teens with the skills and opportunities to make lasting impacts in their community. As a youth-led, co-ed venturing crew under the Piedmont Council BSA, founded 18 years ago, we provide many leadership and volunteer opportunities that cater to most interests, in a lowstress, fun and nurturing environment. Middle school kids and their parents may register with the companion Piedmont Service Club (PSC) where they partake in everything offered by PCSC that is age appropriate. PCSC partners with organizations across the Bay Area to create dynamic and diverse volunteering events multiple times each week. These range from cooking meals for people in underserved communities, building and renovating homes, working with underserved children, and nature immersive clean-up projects. We remain active over summers, striving to have a summer service trip that is planned by our youth. Together, our members gain various skills and experiences that bring them closer into becoming well-rounded individuals in our community. One of PCSC’s most popular events is the annual project with Rebuilding Together Oakland (RTO). Each year 100 or more crew members collectively put in over 1,000 hours into renovating an elderly person’s home in Oakland. Through this project participants learn a range of skills, from fundraising, project planning and teamwork; structural repairs, improvements and then cleaning and repainting the entire house. Above all, crew members learn the value of gratitude and giving back as they work with the homeowner. PCSC members Vale Prieto Black, Elena Stevens, Klara Zietlow, and Sofia Prieto Black describe the work the Crew does and the many benefits for its teen members. articles.text: It’s game week! The Piedmont High football season officially gets underway this Friday, August 26, when hosting Seaside at 7:00 p.m. at Witter Field. It marks the Piedmont debut of firstyear head coach Jordan Seiden. “Our theme this week is ‘focus and finish.’ Focus on the game, focus on what’s in front of us and finish every rep and all of our kids to contribute in some form or fashion,” said Seiden. “We have a good group of kids and are learning fast, their confidence is high, and people are feeling good.” Piedmont will play this season as an independent school this fall after dropping from the Western Alameda County Conference after debate arose about whether to continue the varsity program in 2022 due to low signups. The team will return to the WACC in 2023. This year’s team is still light on numbers, with only around 20 players available throughout training camp. It’s going to require contributions from every player on the team, including those playing varsity football for the first time. “I expect most if not all of our kids to play and participate. It’s going to be a big moment; we have several players who haven’t played high school football before. We’re going to count on some of those kids and we really believe they can handle their responsibility and do their job,” said Seiden. Seiden’s offense will be in the “pro-style” mold. They have been progressively installing their system throughout the summer with this week driving home what to expect on Friday. “It’s good. They are picking up stuff fast. It’s helpful that we run a pretty modern offense with similar concepts to last year but with our own twists. articles.text: Piedmont High senior A.J. Harris has been plugging through the summer and offseason with his AAU basketball club, the Lakeshow. On Saturday, August 20 at Modesto Christian High School, the former school of twins Courtney and Ashley Paris and their siblings. Harris won a 3-point shootout against some of the best players in the state. He’s been working hard at his craft since last winter’s season, studying film, and putting in plenty of hours on the court. “It was definitely nice to get some recognition because I’ve spent a lot of hours working on my shot. I go early in the morning before school at the YMCA just working on my shot. There’s also a lot of other aspects that go into shooting, like watching film on my form and try to fix any issues I see. There’s also a lot of mental game to it, learning to not get frustrated when things aren’t going in.” “It’s nice to get some recognition as one of the best shooters in NorCal,” said Harris. The shootout featured four rounds in a first-to-11 buckets format, resulting in Harris defeating Jamari Phillips of Modesto Christian 11-8. Phillips is rated as a four-star recruit by 247Sports, which slots him in as the No. 19 overall player in the U.S. “I played against Jamari Phillips, who is one grade below me. He’s [being looked at] by some major schools in the country, like Oregon, Texas Tech, Gonzaga, and Kansas. He’s a super good player,” said Harris. Simply Basketball, the organizer, also hosted a game called the Battle of Norcal, where Harris represented the Bay Area and helped them reach the Finals. “I was on team Bay and we played against the best players from the Central area. In the championship, we played against the best players from Stockton. I felt like I was able to hold my own and show that’s where I belong,” said Harris. During the offseason, Harris has been training with Lakeshow, an AAU team with several Piedmont players, JoJo Murphy, Luke Barrett, and older brother Luke Harris. Last June, Harris dominated Vanden by scoring 53 points, 11 rebounds, and three assists. PHS senior A.J. Harris recently won a 3-point shootout hosted at Modesto Christian High School “I’ve just been working on my conditioning, my ball-handling skills, quickness, and being more athletic in order to guard more point guards. Playing with Lakeshow and AAU in the summer is a huge bonus and super helpful to prepare for the season. You travel around the West Coast to play some of the best players out there who have major offers. You can’t be scared of anything and it teaches you to be tough,” said Harris. Aside from competing with Lakeshow, Harris has been spending time perfecting his shot by working with his father Jason Harris, the assistant coach at Piedmont. “I’ve been training a lot with my dad. Ever since I was little, he’s helped me. He was a really good shooter when he was younger, so he’s helped me get my form in the right place. Whenever he notices something I can work on, we’ll just go to the gym and get a bunch of shots up to identify whatever is wrong,” said Harris. Harris is a four-year varsity member and three-year starter with the Highlanders. He mentioned that his goal for the upcoming winter season is to help bring home another North Coast Section title to Piedmont after watching the 2020 team win one as a freshman on the bench. “When I was a freshmen, I played JV and was called up to the varsity team for the playoffs. articles.text: Piedmont High senior Audrey Lam has accomplished something all soccer players strive to achieve – being a member of their national team. Lam qualified for the Under-17 U.S. Women’s National Team earlier this summer, and currently is playing international friendlies in Madrid against the national teams of Spain and Germany. Lam played her first match against Spain yesterday, August 23, and will play the Spanish squad again on Thursday, August 25, before facing Germany on Wednesday, August 31. She played 30 minutes in Tuesday’s match, which the U.S. won 2-0. “It’s everything I’ve dreamed of,” said Lam recently. “Ever since I was little, my goal was to be on the National Team, and this is just one step closer to achieving that goal. I’ve worked pretty hard and this just shows that. It’s really just a dream, I feel honored to be given this opportunity,” said Lam. Her inclusion in the lineup is possibly an auspicious sign. The U-17 FIFA Women’s World Cup is in India October 11-30. Many of the current U.S. players recently competed in the CONCACAF Women’s tournament in May. “I’m looking forward to playing with these players and against these other teams. This leads to the U17 World Cup and hopefully if I play well, I’ll get called up again. As long as I stay disciplined and focused, I think I can achieve this,” said Lam. This marks her second opportunity with the U.S. Women’s National Team after taking part in a U-15 development camp in Kansas City in 2019. It is her first time competing in games with the team. To be called up to the U-17 team, Lam credits impressing coaches at a showcase in Oceanside earlier this summer where she scored three times and turned the heads of coaches. “I practice four times a week with my club and practice by myself as much as I can outside of practice, and it all leads up to the showcases. This past summer at Oceanside. a few scouts came out. I just tried to put everything out there. I tried to show my footwork and I think that got their attention, I scored a few times, which is something they obviously like to see,” said Lam. Lam trains with Lamorinda Soccer Club and competes on their Women’s Soccer Premier League team, Lamorinda United, Audrey Lam, Class of 2023, is currently competing abroad in three international friendlies with the U-17 United States Women’s National Team. Audrey Lam (No. 7) is a central attacking midfielder and plays on Lamorinda Soccer Club’s WPSL team. under head coach Mohamed Mohamed. He’s been coaching Lam for six years and says Lam is a player who makes “everyone better.” Audrey Lam competed on the Piedmont High team last winter and earned first-team All-League honors. “She is extremely talented and a hard worker, not just offensively but defensively as well. She’s the type of player who other players look up to. She’s an extremely humble person and the type of athlete that you want to have on your team. She’s an amazing teammate and we are so proud of her to reach this level and also watch her grow,” said Mohamed. Lam is currently committed to play collegiately at Brown University in Rhode Island with plans of playing professionally and one day making the senior U.S. Women’s National Team. “My goal was to always be on the National Team or go professional. Another goal is to play collegiately and get my degree. After I graduate, my goal is to play professionally wherever I can in the U.S. or Europe, and hopefully continue with the National Team,” said Lam.

articles.text: What inside sources at the club are saying about the move A huge development occurred on Thursday, August 18, with Oakland Roots announcing that they placed their head coach Juan Guerra on administrative leave. This came shortly after Phoenix Rising FC mutually parted ways with its coach Rick Schantz the previous day. Sources indicated to The Post that Phoenix had been engaged in discussions with Guerra without permission. He is under contract with Oakland Roots SC, which deemed it “disruptive to the organization.” The news came one month after it was initially reported that Guerra was a candidate for the Phoenix job, and the wheels have seemingly been turning since then. Two days ago, on Monday, August 22, Phoenix officially announced Guerra had been hired as its new head coach. Oakland Roots stated in a press released that it had come to an agreement to part ways with its former coach after releasing him from his contract. Sources indicate that Oakland received an extensive offer from Phoenix, which included purchasing his remaining contract, buying assistant coach Marcos Reina, and giving Roots rights to allocated roster slots that value at over $200,000. But all this raises the question of what tampering standards were breached by Phoenix Rising FC contacting and negotiating a deal with Guerra while he was under contract. Bylaws of USL Championship, the league in which both teams play, states “players, agents, or representatives cannot engage in any contract negotiations other than with the players’ current club in regards to a future deal.” The rules further state that the league may prohibit the club or player from entering an agreement and may declare the deal null and void. It is unclear if the same bylaws pertain to manager contracts as well. The mood at the Roots’ practice this week was described as “tense” by a source, detailing huddled discussions by the former coaching staff earlier this week, with some coaches canceling team meetings during the buildup to Thursday’s announcement. With nine games left in the season and Oakland four points away from a playoff spot, the announcement couldn’t have come at a more awkward time. Roots center back Tarek Morad voiced some displeasure on Twitter earlier on Tuesday, August 23: “The dogs keep barking, but the train keeps moving.” According to one source, members of the Roots weren’t made fully aware of the situation until Guerra was placed on leave. The Roots will move forward after the appointment of Noah Delgado as interim head coach. He comes with a healthy coaching pedigree. Delgado, 42, was a member of Oakland’s staff last year as an assistant and is the only holdover from last year’s staff. He is also a member of the El Salvador National Team’s coaching staff as an assistant under manager Hugo Perez—a Bay Area legend in the soccer community. Delgado, a native of Fremont, played at Fresno State. He has five years of experience on the Puerto Rico National Team from 2008-2012 as a midfielder, scoring nine goals in 25 appearances. Professionally, he was drafted by the Los Angeles Galaxy with the No. 48 overall pick in the 2002 MLS SuperDraft, but was not offered a contract. Delgado quickly signed with the Portland Timbers in the USL A-League before playing for the Syracuse Salty Dogs and Rochester Raging Rhinos the following two years. From there, he signed with the Puerto Rico Islanders in 2005 and played until their dissolution in 2012, making 174 appearances and scored 16 goals. They made the CONCACAF Champions League Quarterfinals in 2008 and was their captain from 2009- 2011. In 2014, Delgado played for the San Francisco Stompers of the NPSL. articles.text: American Conservatory Theatre (ACT) presents Passengers onstage at the Geary Theatre in San Francisco beginning September 15. The production will run through October 9. Shana Carroll, the creator, director, and choreographer of Passengers, is originally from the Bay Area. The production combines contemporary dance with circus acrobatics, weaving together a story that explores a community of strangers. “When first creating Passengers four years ago, it was in great hope and anticipation of one day, finally, bringing it back home to my native Bay Area. The pandemic put that dream temporarily on hold, but I’m thrilled that – a few long-awaited years later – my little train has finally made its way back to its home station in my beloved San Francisco,” said Carroll. “The themes at the heart of this show – of travel, of nostalgia for foreign lands and past eras, of celebrating a ‘ride’ that is unexpected and so often cut too short ­ – have brought new layers of meaning and importance in our post-pandemic era. In many ways it feels we are premiering a whole new show.” The Geary Theater is located at 415 Geary Street in San Francisco. Tickets are available by calling the box office at (415) 749-2228, or by purchasing online at https://www.act-sf. org/whats-on/202223-season/ passengers/. articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre is currently showing Goddess from the critically-acclaimed team that created New York’s Shakespeare in the Park’s production of Merry Wise. Performances continue through September. Goddess is inspired by the myth of Marimba, the goddess of music, and an ancient folktale passed down by many generations across the continent of Africa. According to the folktale, Marimba created the first instruments and was the first to use her voice in song. She is also described as the most beautiful woman who ever existed and an advocate for peace, she refashioned weapons into instruments and opposed the violence of war. The play was conceived by Saheem Ali, based on a book by Jocelyn Bioh. Music and Lyrics are by Michael Thurber, and choreographed by Darrell Grand Moultrie. The cast includes Awa Sal Secka, Aaron Patterson, Isio-Maya Nuwere, Grasan Kingsberry, Rodrick Covington, Melessie Clark, Wade Watson and Zachary Downer. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/goddess/.

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse is currently performing the musical Follies through September 10. The show is based on a book of the same name written by James Goldman, with music and lyrics by Stephen Sondheim. Goldman was an American playwright, novelist, and screenwriter, whose first play on Broadway was a comedy about life in the army, Blood, Sweat, and Stanley Poole (1961). Follies opened on Broadway in 1971 to critical acclaim. It was nominated for 11 Tony awards and won seven. The play focuses on two couples, Buddy and Sally Durant Plummer and Benjamin and Phyllis Rogers Stone, who are attending the reunion of crumbling theatre. Sally and Phyllis, the lead characters, are showgirls in the Follies and both in failing marriages. Cast members include Caroline Altman, Catrina Manahan, Samantha Rose Cárdenas, Ann Warque, Danielle Cheiken, Emily Corbo, Rene Collins, Chachi Delgado, M.Javi Harnly, and Catrina Manahan. articles.text: Hey, George. The first thing we need to do is to confirm your credentials. You were a music critic, weren’t you? My name is Bernard. articles.text: A scene from Cloudy With a Chance of Meatballs. Cloudy With a Chance of Meatballs was released in 2009 and adapted from the children’s book by Judi and Ron Barrett. The story is set in the small town of Swallow Falls. For years its economy has been dependent on catching and selling sardines. But unexpectedly the demand for sardines takes a steep dive and the denizens of Swallow Falls find themselves with an economic problem. To the rescue comes Flint Hardwood (Bill Harder), a bright teen who loves to invent stuff like spray on shoes, or a television with legs that can walk over to you if you want to change the channel. Flint’s gruff dad, Tim (James Caan), owns a bait and tackle shop and is feeling the effects of the lack of demand for sardines on his business. Flint puts his inventing cap on and decides he wants to help the town and sets about creating a machine that converts water into food. Somehow his invention is suspended in the sky (don’t ask), and when it starts to rain, well, it’s not rain but cheeseburgers, hotdogs, soup and mashed potatoes, jell-O molds that kids can bounce on, and any other type of food Flint orders from his computer. The folks of Swallow Falls are delighted, especially the town’s youngsters who get to enjoy a morning snow fall of ice cream. Plus there’s Sam Sparks (Anna Faris), a local weather girl, who is a bit confused about what to forecast. And there’s the ever-hungry Swallow Falls mayor (Bruce Campbell) who can’t wait for the next food storm. But, as things turn out, the residents get greedy and begin demanding bigger portions. As a result, Flint’s machine begins to go a bit haywire and strange things begin to happen. There’s a tornado of spaghetti, a blizzard of sherbet, a pancake falls on top of the school, and a giant cob of corn rolls downhill after a group terrified kids. Cloudy With a Chance of Meatballs is a lot of fun, filled with gags, interesting characters, and, of course, a few life lessons, such as follow your dream, believe in yourself, and know that your grumpy old dad, Tim, actually does love you. Cloudy With a Chance of Meatballs. Directed by Chris Miller and Phil Lord. Voiced by Bill Harder, Anna Faris, Andy Sandberg, and James Caan. Animated. 1 hr., 30 min. Rated PG. Released in 2009. Now streaming on Netflix/Prime/VUDU.

articles.text: Will Ferrell has constructed a successful career playing outrageous, exaggerated, slapstick caricatures. Recall Anchorman: The Legend of Ron Burgundy, Step Brothers, or Talladega Nights. He has perfected the deer-caughtin-the headlights moment, the comedic intersection between plain, dumb obliviousness and a grudging, cranky awareness and has found a fan base. Ferrell has done straight drama far too infrequently. Surprisingly, he is an actor who can portray a certain character with subtlety and insight, pathos and humanity, as he so nicely demonstrated in Stranger Than Fiction, and in Everything Must Go. In fact, it could be argued that some of his best work is to be found in these two films and not in those banal comedies he has starred in following his years on Saturday Night Live. In Everything Must Go, his character, Nick Halsey, is a study in sadness, touched by an existential despair. He arrives home after an awful day – he’s been fired from his job as a mid-level sales executive because of an alleged drunken episode with a female employee and his ongoing battle with alcoholism – and finds the locks on his house changed and all of his stuff, soup to nuts, on the front lawn, including his favorite recliner. His marriage, evidently, is over and he has been moved out, if no further than the lawn. It’s his quiet and deliberate response that makes this film appealing. He begins to arrange all of the items as if the lawn were his rec room, then heads off to the local liquor store and buys two twelve packs of beer. He returns to his lawn and his recliner where he sits, contemplating his life and future. Such as it is. What’s intriguing about Nick is that he neither rages, nor becomes maudlin; instead, he drinks a beer (and then another and then another) and looks out at his neighbors, feigning a studied sense of normalcy – I now live outside the house and not inside the house – though life has dealt him a crushing defeat, his loneliness suddenly defined with a brutal clarity. Clearly it’s time to make some changes, and he starts by unloading his stuff, a metaphor for so much that has cluttered up his life and gotten in his way, perhaps insulating him from who he is, which, as it turns out, is a pretty decent guy. Good narrative cinema is rare. So much of what is sold by Hollywood as substantive is nonsense, likely based on the premise that character driven films will not attract an audience. Our loss. Based on a Raymond Carver short story, Everything Must Go is an evocative film, nuanced and engaging, an examination of life and the human condition, such as it is. As well, Ferrell is working with a talented ensemble of actors to include Rebecca Hall, a pregnant neighbor who is waiting for her husband to arrive from New York; Christopher Wallace as a young, at-loose-ends kid whose mother works in the neighborhood; Michael Pena, portraying Nick’s AA sponsor and a Scottsdale detective; and Stephen Root, delivering a nice cameo as a tightly-wound next-door neighbor. They’re all top drawer. Everything Must Go. Starring Will Ferrell, Rebecca Hall, Laura Dern and Stephen Root. Written and directed by Dan Rush. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated R. Released in 2011. Now streaming on Prime/ Netflix/VUDU.

Northern Tier is a canoe-based High Adventure trip offered by Scouts BSA, with separate locations in Minnesota and Canada. We planned a trip to the Manitoba base, deep in the buggy lowlands and miles away from the closest town because it was the most challenging and rugged of all the bases. Our roster of seven Scouts and four parents was decided in mid-2021, when we began getting gear, establishing training exercises, treating clothes with bug repellent, and reading emails rivaling libraries in their magnitude. We met often to discuss different aspects of our travel plans while also practice canoeing on Lake Merritt and at Del Valle. Early morning Zoom meetings to schedule flights were commonplace as the trip grew nearer. On Friday, July 15, we boarded a plane to Vancouver, then Winnipeg, where we stayed in a hotel overnight. GOOD THROUGH SEPTEMBER 2022 GOOD THROUGH SEPTEMBER 2022 GOOD THROUGH SEPTEMBER 2022 The journey started with a float plane ride to Scout Lake. town in the north of Manitoba. There we met our guide, Matt, and went over the gear we had brought, which was packed down into impossibly small waterproof bags. We charted our course across the wilderness (60 miles total) in the Map Room, and prepared our crew’s gear before spending our final night in relative comfort on the base. The next morning, we quickly packed our gear and walked to a small lakeside dock. A floatplane came for us, and we were treated to an unforgettable and beautiful view of the untouched Canadian wilderness as we left civilization behind. Landing at Scout Lake, we retrieved our canoes from a cache and were off after some quick lessons in paddling and portaging, which consists of carrying the boat on one’s shoulders over land. Our convoy was made up of four canoes, with three people to each one. Paddlers in the back were responsible for steering the canoe, while paddlers in the front powered the boat forward. In the middle was the “duff” seat, where one just sits and navigates. We quickly got used to the rhythm of paddling, and our first few portages went off without a hitch. Little did we know, howGOOD THROUGH SEPTEMBER 2022 ever, what was in store for us at our campsite. Our first night was spent on Lake Noname, on a mossy outcropping of a campsite. After bringing our canoes ashore and setting up camp, we began a read-aloud of the Princess Bride as storm clouds brewed in the distance. Less than an hour later we awoke to the most torrential downpour any of us had ever seen. Completely drenched, we retreated to our tents ready to spend the rest of the night cold and damp in our sleeping bags. Minutes later the rain stopped and was replaced by a gorgeous sunset. I suddenly knew what he meant when Matt told us this would be the best and hardest trip of our lives. The next few days were similarly action-packed. Day two’s calm waters were interrupted by a few baby rapids. I managed to nearly capsize my boat and fling our adult leader into the water. Day three’s camp was on the shores of the enormous Lake Sasaginnigak, where we spent an idyllic afternoon drying out clothes, catching fish, and swimming to nearby islands.

articles.text: Editor: Over the last 50+ years that my family has lived in Piedmont, we have seen progressive changes in the city’s demographics. Our family moved to Piedmont in 1967 when most parents were having children when they were in their 20s and comfortably suviving on one salary. Today the social and economic structures of families in our community have drastically changed. For a majority of our city, two full-time incomes are often needed to purchase a home in Piedmont, and even with dual incomes, many of my fellow alumni returning to our community still needed help from their parents to purchase their homes. Enrollment in schools is drastically declining, reflecting young adults delaying parenthood until they can simultaneously afford a house and childcare in a city that doesn’t cater to working families. Many of our longer-term residents who raised children here couldn’t afford to purchase their own homes at today’s current rates. The need for more affordable housing in Piedmont for families, seniors, school, and city employees is critical. For all these reasons and many more, I believe we should embrace additional, yet gentle density housing in Piedmont as the state is requiring us to do. I agree with those who have voiced concerns about over-development. I believe we don’t need to drastically change the look or feel of Piedmont. We could add small multi-family units on top of the buildings already in dire need of structural upgrades, such as our city center, the plethora of antiquated and almost always empty brick-and-mortar banks, as well as Grand Avenue. Replacing the ever growing list of dilapidated and abandoned homes in Piedmont with affordable multifamily units would improve home values more than the homes with tarps covering the holes in the roofs and plywood over their broken windows. I want young people in their 20s and 30s to be able to move to Piedmont and eventually afford a home here. The problems we are experiencing are not unique. I would like to see Piedmont looking to the future to see how the benefits of creating more housing would strengthen the fabric of our community. I want our future generations to see that Piedmonters are wise, creative, and forward-thinking. Curriculum Director Cheryl Wozniak and a school board member conducted the second round of interviews. Edible contests have been a part of the Piedmont Harvest Festival since the beginning in 1998. They showcase, for the appreciation of all, the amazing diversity of fruits and vegetables grown in Piedmont, and the talent of our residents in preparing and preserving these products for their families and friends. Eligibility Anyone who lives or works in the City of Piedmont may submit an entry. Entries may be done by individuals, households, neighborhoods or groups. Rules of Entry Any item submitted for consideration in a growing category must be grown within the borders of the City of Piedmont, CA. Any item that is submitted for a cooking category must have a main ingredient that could feasibly be grown in Piedmont. The actual ingredient does not have to have been grown within the borders of Piedmont. Items submitted for display only are not limited by the above rules. Non-residents are welcome to join the fun by bringing items for display only. No Fees There is no charge to enter. Prizes All participants will receive recognition and prizes will vary among categories. The Bill Drum Memorial Sweepstakes Prize is awarded to the person or group that receives the most blue ribbons. Number of Entries Any number of entries are allowed in each category by individuals or groups. Submission of Entries All entries must be delivered between 7:30am and 10:00am on Sunday, September 19, 2021 Please bring your completed entry form (or proof of digital submission) to the Community Hall. Use one entry form for all entries and be sure a label is securely attached for each entry. Labels for items in the cooking categories must have the "main ingredient" clearly visible. Additional forms are available at the Recreation Department, City Hall, or at www.piedmont.ca.gov Judging Judges for the contest will be knowledgeable in the areas they judge. Entrants are reminded of the objective of the Festival: to provide an opportunity for people to show the bounty of their gardens and kitchens, to provide a source of fun and to strengthen our sense of community. Judging begins promptly at 10:00am and is not open to the public. Any Item Not Picked Up by 1:30pm Will be Eaten or Recycled Due care will be taken to insure the safety of entries during the festival. However, neither the Recreation Department nor the Harvest Festival Committee can assume responsibility for any loss or damage that may occur. Entries will be cleared at 1:30pm Make Scarecrow Any individual or group (resident or non-resident) can make a scarecrow and donate it for the Silent Auction. Scarecrows must be family-friendly and proceeds will benefit the Tri-School Fund.
